blocks.prompt: The Plant On Your Plate
blocks.text: Plants have parts. Roots. Stems. Leaves. Flowers. Seeds. Every vegetable you eat is one of those parts. A carrot is a root. It stores food for the plant, deep in the soil. Celery is a stem. It is the stalk that holds the plant up. Lettuce is leaves. Cabbage is leaves too, packed in a tight ball. Broccoli is a bunch of tiny flower buds. If you left it in the garden, it would open up and bloom yellow. Peas are seeds. Each pea could grow into a new plant. So a plate of vegetables is really a pile of plant parts. Roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and seeds, all mixed together.

3.title: Nobody Grows a Vegetable

blocks.prompt: A Kitchen Word, Not a Plant Word
blocks.text: Ask a gardener what a vegetable is and you will get a strange answer. There is no such thing. Plants do not grow vegetables. Plants grow roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and seeds. Vegetable is a word people made up in the kitchen. It just means a plant part we like to eat with dinner. Once you know that, the vegetable drawer gets interesting. A carrot is a root, fat with stored food. Celery is a stem. Lettuce and cabbage are leaves. Broccoli is a crowd of flower buds, picked before they can open. Leave broccoli in the garden for two more weeks and it turns into a spray of small yellow flowers. Peas and beans are seeds. A potato is not a root at all. It is a swollen underground stem, which is why it grows little eyes that can sprout. So dinner is a plant taken apart. Roots on one side of the plate, leaves on the other, flower buds in the middle, and nobody at the table thinking about it.

4.title: Nobody Grows a Vegetable
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Brassica oleracea: one species, six vegetables
Kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi, sprouts
Wild cabbage still grows on European sea cliffs
Selective breeding is thousands of years old
Kale and cabbage can still be crossed

blocks.prompt: Six Vegetables, One Plant
blocks.text: On the sea cliffs of Europe grows a scruffy, bitter plant called wild cabbage. It is nobody's idea of dinner. Tough leaves, a woody stalk, a spray of pale flowers. And yet almost everything on the vegetable shelf that your family argues about came out of it. Thousands of years ago, farmers began choosing. A farmer who liked the leaves saved seeds from the leafiest plants, and planted those, and did it again the next year, and the next. After enough generations of choosing, the leaves grew huge. That plant is kale. Another farmer kept choosing plants with a tight bud at the top. That became cabbage. Choose the flower buds instead and you get broccoli. Keep choosing broccoli for fatter, paler, tighter heads and you get cauliflower. Choose the swollen stem and you get kohlrabi. Choose the little buds along the stalk and you get brussels sprouts. Kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi, brussels sprouts. Six vegetables that taste nothing alike and look nothing alike. They are all the same species: Brassica oleracea. They can still be crossed with each other, the way two dogs of different breeds can. A great dane and a chihuahua are one species too, shaped by the same slow patience. This is called selective breeding, and it is one of the oldest technologies humans have. No lab, no machines. Just a farmer, a handful of seeds, and the decision about which plant gets to have children.

5.title: Nobody Grows a Vegetable
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Glucosinolates: the cabbage family's chemical defense
Bitterness is released when leaves are chewed
TAS2R38: a bitter-taste gene
Kids have more taste buds than adults
Sprouts were bred milder in the 1990s
Bitter sensitivity fades with age

blocks.prompt: The Taste of a Plant Fighting Back
blocks.text: Here is a fact that might rearrange your dinner table: broccoli is trying to stop you. A plant cannot run. It cannot hide, bite back, or call for help. When something starts eating it, a plant has one option left, which is chemistry. Over millions of years, plants in the cabbage family evolved a group of compounds called glucosinolates. When a leaf is crushed or chewed, those compounds break apart and release a sharp, bitter, sulfur taste. To a caterpillar, that taste is a warning label. To you, it is the reason brussels sprouts are an argument. So the bitterness is not a flaw in the vegetable. It is the vegetable's defense, working exactly as designed, on the wrong animal. Kids get a stronger dose of the warning. Human children have more taste buds than adults do, and many people carry a version of a gene called TAS2R38 that makes bitter compounds taste intensely, almost violently bitter. Two people can chew the same sprout and honestly disagree about what happened. Neither is lying. Sensitivity to bitterness also tends to fade with age, which is why adults claim to like foods that children find inedible, and why they are not entirely making it up. Then people did something about it. In the 1990s, a Dutch plant scientist named Hans van Doorn identified the specific compounds behind the bitterness of brussels sprouts. Breeders went back to old seed varieties that were naturally low in those compounds, crossed them with modern high-yield plants, and slowly produced a sprout that tastes mild. The brussels sprouts sold today are genuinely not the ones your grandparents refused. The vegetable changed. The complaint stayed. It is worth noticing what that story is really about. For ten thousand years, plants have been evolving chemicals to keep from being eaten, and humans have been quietly editing those chemicals back out. The sprout on your plate is one move in an argument that has been going on longer than writing.

6.title: Nobody Grows a Vegetable
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Vegetable is a culinary category, not a botanical one
Nix v. Hedden, 1893: the tomato ruled a vegetable
Potato is a tuber, a swollen underground stem
Brassica oleracea: kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi, sprouts
Early cultivated carrots were purple and yellow
Tomato, cucumber, pepper, eggplant are botanically fruits

blocks.prompt: The Category Nobody Planted
blocks.text: Nature does not grow vegetables. It grows roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and seeds, and it grows them for its own reasons, none of which involve dinner. The word vegetable does not describe a plant part, a plant family, or anything a botanist could point to under a microscope. It describes a decision people made about where a plant belongs on a plate. It is a kitchen category wearing a lab coat. Follow that idea and the produce aisle comes apart in your hands. A carrot is a taproot, a swollen storage organ the plant filled with sugar to survive the winter. Celery is a stem. Lettuce is leaves. Broccoli is a dense crowd of unopened flower buds, harvested days before it would have bloomed. Peas are seeds, each one a packed lunch for a plant that never got the chance to start. A potato is not a root but a tuber, an underground stem, which is why it sprouts eyes and why gardeners can grow a new plant from a chunk of the old one. Meanwhile the tomato, the cucumber, the pepper, the pumpkin, and the eggplant are all botanically fruits: seed-bearing structures grown from a flower. We simply do not eat them with sugar, so we filed them somewhere else. This confusion has been to court. In 1893, in a case called Nix v. Hedden, the United States Supreme Court had to decide whether tomatoes were fruits or vegetables, because imported vegetables were taxed and fruits were not. The Court agreed that a tomato is botanically a fruit. It ruled that it is legally a vegetable anyway, on the grounds that people eat it with dinner and not for dessert. Science lost to habit, unanimously. But the strangest part is not that we invented the category. It is that we then built the things to fill it. On the sea cliffs of Europe grows wild cabbage, a tough and bitter weed. Kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi, and brussels sprouts are all the same species as that weed, Brassica oleracea, pulled into six different shapes by farmers who spent centuries saving seed from whichever plant leaned in the direction they wanted. Choose leaves and you get kale. Choose the terminal bud and you get cabbage. Choose the flower buds and you get broccoli. Carrots tell a similar story: the earliest cultivated carrots were purple and yellow, and the orange carrot that now defines the word did not become standard until European growers favored it a few hundred years ago. The vegetable you picture when you hear the word is a recent human product. So when someone says a vegetable is healthy, or bitter, or boring, they are not describing nature. They are describing ten thousand years of human choices about which plants deserved to have children. The category is invented. The contents are engineered. And the only part of the whole arrangement the plant ever agreed to is the part where it tried to defend itself, which we bred out, because we did not like the taste.
